title: Membrane Potentials and the Action Potential
subject: Human Physiology
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie
intro: Work each activity on blank paper with your notes closed, then open the key and mark what you missed. Do the two brain dumps for one competency on separate days instead of back to back.

activities.title: Draw the resting membrane and label what sets it
activities.prompt: Without looking at your notes, draw a section of a neuron membrane with the inside on one side and the outside on the other. Write the resting membrane potential of a typical neuron in millivolts and say what the minus sign in front of that number means. Place the four ions that matter here, sodium, potassium, chloride and the negatively charged proteins, on the side where each one is more concentrated. Then write three short reasons the inside sits negative at rest: which ion the resting membrane leaks most easily and which channel lets it out, which ion is kept out because few of its channels are open at rest, and which particles are stuck inside because they are too large to cross. Finish by defining resting membrane potential in one sentence a classmate would understand.

activities.title: Move the resting potential and say which way
activities.prompt: A neuron is sitting at its normal resting potential. One at a time, work through these four changes and for each one write whether the membrane potential moves closer to zero or further below zero, name the direction of that move using the words depolarization or hyperpolarization, and give the reason in one sentence. First, the potassium concentration outside the cell rises. Second, extra potassium leak channels open. Third, a few sodium channels open while the cell is still at rest. Fourth, the fluid around the cell is replaced with a solution that has no sodium in it at all. For the fourth one, also write whether you would expect the resting potential to change much and explain your answer.

activities.title: Draw the sodium potassium pump at work
activities.prompt: Draw the sodium potassium pump in a membrane. Write how many sodium ions it moves and in which direction, how many potassium ions it moves and in which direction, and what molecule it spends to do it. Write the net charge the pump moves out of the cell with each cycle and say in one sentence how that small charge movement adds to the negative resting potential. Then write the approximate concentration of sodium and of potassium inside the cell and outside the cell, and beside each pair draw an arrow showing which way that ion would drift if a channel for it opened. Last, define the term concentration gradient in your own words and say which structure builds and maintains these two gradients.

activities.title: Lose the pump and follow the consequences
activities.prompt: A cell is poisoned so its sodium potassium pumps stop working, but every channel in the membrane still works normally. Write what happens over the next several minutes to the sodium concentration inside the cell, the potassium concentration inside the cell, the size of each gradient, and the resting membrane potential. Then write whether the cell can still fire one action potential right after the pump stops and explain why, and whether it can still fire them an hour later and explain why. Finish with two sentences on why physiologists call the gradients a stored supply of energy for the cell.

activities.title: Predict what rising outside potassium does
activities.prompt: The potassium concentration in the fluid around a neuron climbs from its normal value to well above normal. For each item below, write whether it increases, decreases or stays the same, then write one sentence of reasoning that names the gradient or the channel involved. Do not look anything up until you have written all five.
changes: The size of the potassium concentration gradient across the membrane
The rate at which potassium leaks out of the cell at rest
The resting membrane potential, stated as closer to zero or further below zero
How close the membrane sits to the threshold voltage
The number of voltage gated sodium channels that are able to open when a stimulus arrives

activities.title: Two kinds of electrical signal, side by side
activities.prompt: Draw two sets of axes with voltage on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. On the first, sketch a graded potential, meaning a small local change in membrane voltage. On the second, sketch an action potential, meaning the large all or nothing signal a neuron sends down its axon. Beside each drawing write where on the neuron it normally happens, what opens the channels that cause it, roughly how large it is in millivolts, how far it travels before it fades, and whether its size can vary with the strength of the stimulus. Then define threshold in one sentence and mark it on the second drawing. Last, write what the phrase all or nothing means and why it applies to only one of these two signals.

activities.title: From small inputs to a fired axon
activities.prompt: Three small depolarizing graded potentials arrive at one neuron. Write what happens at the start of the axon in each of these situations and give your reason each time. First, the three arrive one after another with long gaps between them. Second, the three arrive at nearly the same moment at the same spot on the dendrite. Third, the three arrive at the same moment but at three spots far apart on the dendrites. Fourth, two depolarizing graded potentials and one hyperpolarizing graded potential arrive together. Then answer this: a stimulus is doubled in strength and the neuron is already firing. Write what changes in the signal the axon sends, since the height of each action potential cannot change, and name the feature of the signal that carries stimulus strength instead.

activities.title: Graded potential compared with action potential
activities.prompt: Fill in every cell of the table from memory, in short phrases rather than sentences. Leave no cell blank; if you are unsure, write your best answer and circle it so you can check it against the key.
rows: Where on the neuron it usually occurs
What causes the channels to open
Main ion or ions that move
Typical size of the voltage change
Does size vary with stimulus strength
How far it travels and whether it fades
Does it need to reach threshold

activities.title: Draw the action potential and label every gate
activities.prompt: Draw one action potential with voltage on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. Mark the resting potential, the threshold voltage, the peak voltage, and the lowest point of the undershoot, and write a number in millivolts beside each one. Label these parts on your drawing: the graded depolarization up to threshold, the rising phase, the peak, the falling phase, and the undershoot, also called hyperpolarization. Beside each part write which channel is opening or closing at that moment, which ion is moving, and which direction that ion is going. For the voltage gated sodium channel, draw both of its gates, name them, and write what each gate is doing at rest, at threshold, at the peak, and during the falling phase. Then write why the potassium channels are described as slow and what that slowness produces at the end of the tracing.

activities.title: Change one gate and redraw the tracing
activities.prompt: Redraw the normal action potential lightly, then on top of it sketch what the tracing looks like in each of these four situations and write one sentence saying why. First, a toxin holds the inactivation gates of the sodium channels open so they never close. Second, a drug slows the voltage gated potassium channels so they open later than normal. Third, half of the voltage gated sodium channels are blocked and cannot open at all. Fourth, the sodium concentration outside the cell is lowered to half of normal. For each one, state what happens to the peak voltage, the length of the action potential, and whether the cell still reaches threshold.

activities.title: Rebuild the action potential step by step
activities.prompt: Rebuild the full sequence of the action potential from memory as a numbered list, one event per line and in order, starting with a stimulus that depolarizes the membrane to threshold and ending with the membrane back at its resting potential. Write at least eight steps. Beside each step name the channel involved, the ion moving, and the direction it moves. Do not draw a graph here; write the sequence in words so you can see whether the order is solid in your memory.
activities.rebuild: The sequence of channel events in one action potential

activities.title: A numb tooth after a dental injection
activities.stem: A healthy 20 year old student has a cavity filled. Before drilling, the dentist injects lidocaine, a local anesthetic, into the gum beside the tooth. Lidocaine crosses the membranes of nearby neurons and binds inside the pore of voltage gated sodium channels, holding them closed. Within a few minutes the student feels nothing sharp in that tooth or in the nearby lip, although she can still move her jaw normally and can still feel firm pressure when the dentist presses on the gum. About two hours later the numbness wears off completely with no lasting damage.
asks: Name which part of the electrical signal the drug stops and state whether the problem is in the resting potential, the graded potential, or the action potential.

Write the mechanism in three or four sentences: what the blocked channel can no longer do, which phase of the action potential disappears, and why the signal therefore never travels along the axon to the brain.
Explain why pain fades first while pressure sensation and jaw movement are still present, using axon diameter and myelin to support your answer.
Write two observations you could make at the chair, without any equipment, that would tell you whether the block has taken effect in sensory axons, and say what each observation shows.
Decide whether the resting membrane potential of the blocked neuron is still normal and state your answer as a single sentence.
Justify that decision by naming which channels and which pump set the resting potential and explaining why a drug that blocks only voltage gated sodium channels leaves it unchanged.

activities.title: The two refractory periods on one tracing
activities.prompt: Draw an action potential and mark the absolute refractory period and the relative refractory period along the time axis. Define each one in a single sentence, where absolute means no second action potential is possible no matter how strong the stimulus and relative means a second one is possible but needs a stronger stimulus than usual. Beside the absolute refractory period write the state of both sodium channel gates and say which gate is responsible. Beside the relative refractory period write what the slow potassium channels are still doing and why that makes threshold harder to reach. Then write what the sodium channels must do before the cell is fully ready again, and name the voltage range the membrane has to return to for that to happen.

activities.title: Why the signal runs one way and has a speed limit
activities.prompt: An action potential is halfway along an axon. The patch of membrane just behind it has only just finished firing. Write what state the sodium channels in that patch are in and use it to explain why the signal keeps moving forward instead of spreading backward. Next, a researcher stimulates a neuron faster and faster. Write what sets the maximum number of action potentials that neuron can fire in one second and estimate that number if the absolute refractory period lasts about one millisecond. Last, write two sentences on what would go wrong in a muscle or a nerve if refractory periods did not exist at all.

activities.title: Draw a myelinated axon and show how the signal jumps
activities.prompt: Draw a short length of myelinated axon. Label the myelin sheath, one node of Ranvier, meaning a bare gap in the sheath, and the cell that makes myelin in the peripheral nervous system and the one that makes it in the central nervous system. Write what myelin is made of and the two things it does to the axon membrane underneath it. Mark where the voltage gated sodium channels are concentrated. Then show with arrows how the action potential moves from node to node, name that pattern, and write a one sentence definition of it. Finish by listing the two factors that make an axon conduct faster and write the approximate conduction speed of a large myelinated axon and of a small unmyelinated one.

activities.title: Strip the myelin and compare the cost
activities.prompt: An axon loses patches of its myelin while the axon itself stays intact. Write what happens to conduction speed, to whether the signal reaches the end of the axon at all, and to the sensation or movement that axon serves. Explain in two or three sentences why losing the sheath can stop a signal completely rather than only slowing it, using what you know about where the sodium channels sit in a myelinated axon. Then compare two ways a body could build a fast axon, by adding myelin or by making the axon much wider, and write which one costs less space in a nerve and why. Finish by naming the type of axon that carries sharp pain and the type that carries dull aching pain, and say which one is myelinated.

activities.stem: During the absolute refractory period of a neuron, a second stimulus of any strength cannot produce another action potential. Which statement best explains why?
options: The sodium potassium pump has not yet restored the sodium and potassium concentration gradients
The membrane potential is more negative than the resting potential, so threshold is further away
The inactivation gates of the voltage gated sodium channels are closed and will not reopen until the membrane repolarizes
All of the voltage gated potassium channels are closed, so potassium cannot leave the cell

activities.stem: A myelinated axon conducts an action potential far faster than an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter. Which feature of the myelinated axon accounts for most of that difference?
options: Myelin supplies extra ATP to the sodium potassium pumps along the axon
The sheath keeps charge from leaking across the membrane, so the depolarization spreads quickly to the next node of Ranvier, where the sodium channels are clustered
Myelin raises the number of sodium channels spread evenly along the whole length of the axon membrane
The sheath shortens the absolute refractory period so each patch of membrane can fire again sooner

essentials: A typical neuron rests near minus 70 millivolts, and the minus sign means the inside of the cell is negative compared with the outside.
Potassium and the large negatively charged proteins are concentrated inside the cell; sodium and chloride are concentrated outside.
At rest the membrane is far more permeable to potassium than to sodium because potassium leak channels are open, so potassium drifts out down its gradient and leaves negative charge behind.
Few sodium channels are open at rest, so sodium cannot follow its strong inward gradient in large amounts.
Negatively charged proteins and phosphates are trapped inside because they are too large to cross the membrane, which adds to the inside negativity.
Resting membrane potential is the steady voltage difference across the membrane of a cell that is not sending a signal.
distinctions: Permeability is not the same as gradient. Sodium has the larger driving force at rest, but potassium has the open channels, so potassium decides the resting voltage.
Leak channels are always open; voltage gated channels are closed at rest.
misconceptions: Thinking the inside is negative because there is no sodium inside. There is sodium inside, just much less than outside, and the negativity comes from potassium leaving plus the trapped proteins.
Thinking the resting potential means no ions are moving. Ions move constantly at rest; the movements balance.

essentials: Raising outside potassium shrinks the potassium gradient, so less potassium leaves, less negative charge is left behind, and the membrane moves closer to zero, which is depolarization.
Opening extra potassium leak channels lets more potassium out, so the inside becomes more negative and the membrane moves further below zero, which is hyperpolarization.
Opening a few sodium channels lets sodium in down its gradient, adding positive charge inside and depolarizing the membrane.
Removing all outside sodium changes the resting potential very little, because the resting membrane barely lets sodium through in the first place.
distinctions: Depolarization means moving toward zero and beyond; hyperpolarization means moving further from zero in the negative direction.
A change in a gradient matters only if there is an open channel for that ion.
misconceptions: Expecting removal of outside sodium to wipe out the resting potential. It cripples the action potential instead, since the rising phase depends on sodium entry.
key.where: Section 1, what shifts the resting potential

essentials: Each cycle moves three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions in, using one molecule of ATP.
Because three positive charges leave for every two that enter, the pump moves one net positive charge out per cycle and adds a small amount to the inside negativity.
Sodium is about 145 millimoles per liter outside and about 15 inside; potassium is about 4 millimoles per liter outside and about 140 inside.
If a sodium channel opened, sodium would rush in; if a potassium channel opened, potassium would drift out.
A concentration gradient is a difference in the amount of a substance between two places, here across the membrane.
The sodium potassium pump builds and maintains both gradients and runs continuously.
distinctions: The pump is active transport and needs ATP; leak channels and voltage gated channels are passive and need no ATP.
The pump contributes only a few millivolts directly; its main job is keeping the gradients that everything else depends on.
misconceptions: Crediting the pump with the whole resting potential. Most of the voltage comes from potassium leaving through leak channels.
Reversing the direction, saying the pump pushes potassium out. It pulls potassium in.

essentials: With the pump stopped, sodium leaks in and accumulates inside while potassium leaks out and falls inside, so both gradients shrink.
As the potassium gradient shrinks, the resting potential drifts toward zero, meaning the cell slowly depolarizes.
The cell can still fire immediately after the pump stops, because the gradients are still nearly full and one action potential moves only a tiny fraction of the ions present.
An hour later the gradients have run down, so there is no longer enough driving force for sodium to produce a full rising phase and firing fails.
The gradients act as stored energy: the pump spends ATP to build them, and channels later release that stored energy as current when they open.
distinctions: Immediate failure versus gradual failure. Blocking the pump does not stop the next action potential; it stops the hundredth one.
The pump restores gradients over time but does not repolarize the membrane after a spike; potassium channels do that.
misconceptions: Believing the pump reverses each action potential directly. Repolarization is potassium leaving through voltage gated channels, not pump activity.

essentials: The potassium concentration gradient decreases, because the outside value rises toward the inside value.
Potassium leak out of the cell at rest decreases, since the driving force pushing it out is smaller.
The resting membrane potential moves closer to zero, which is depolarization.
The membrane sits closer to threshold, so a smaller stimulus can trigger firing at first.
If depolarization is large or lasting, the number of sodium channels able to open decreases, because sustained depolarization leaves many of them inactivated.
distinctions: A mild rise in outside potassium makes cells easier to excite; a large or sustained rise makes them harder to excite and eventually unexcitable.
Closer to threshold is not the same as more able to fire, because channel availability also matters.
misconceptions: Assuming any depolarization always increases excitability. Past a point the sodium channels sit inactivated and excitability falls.
Thinking raising outside potassium drives potassium into the cell against everything else. It mainly slows the outward leak.

essentials: A graded potential is a small local voltage change, usually in dendrites or the cell body, produced when chemically gated or mechanically gated channels open.
Graded potentials vary in size with stimulus strength, are usually a few millivolts, and fade as they spread away from where they started.
An action potential happens at the axon and travels its full length without fading, swinging from about minus 70 millivolts to about plus 30 millivolts.
Action potentials are produced by voltage gated sodium and potassium channels and occur only if the membrane reaches threshold.
Threshold is the voltage, near minus 55 millivolts, at which enough voltage gated sodium channels open that depolarization becomes self sustaining.
All or nothing means that once threshold is reached the action potential goes to full size every time, and below threshold nothing happens; it applies to the action potential only.
distinctions: Graded potentials decide whether a signal starts; the action potential is the signal that gets sent.
Size varies in graded potentials, while frequency varies in action potentials.
misconceptions: Calling a small depolarization a weak action potential. A subthreshold depolarization is a graded potential, not a small spike.
Thinking the action potential shrinks as it travels down the axon. It is regenerated along the way and arrives full size.
key.where: Section 3, graded potentials and action potentials

essentials: Three inputs spaced far apart in time each fade before the next arrives, so the membrane never reaches threshold and no action potential fires.
Three inputs arriving almost together at one spot add up in time, which is temporal summation, and can reach threshold.
Three inputs arriving together at separate spots add up in space, which is spatial summation, and can also reach threshold.
A hyperpolarizing input subtracts from the depolarizing ones, so the sum may stay below threshold and no action potential fires.
A stronger stimulus raises the firing frequency and may recruit more neurons; the height of each action potential does not change, so frequency codes stimulus strength.
distinctions: Temporal summation is many inputs close in time at one site; spatial summation is inputs at different sites at the same time.
Excitatory inputs depolarize, inhibitory inputs hyperpolarize, and the axon start responds to the running total.
misconceptions: Thinking a bigger stimulus produces a bigger action potential. It produces more action potentials per second.
key.where: Section 3, summation and coding of stimulus strength

essentials: Location: graded potential in dendrites and cell body; action potential at the axon, starting where the axon leaves the cell body.
Trigger: graded potential from chemically gated, mechanically gated or light gated channels; action potential from voltage gated channels once threshold is reached.
Ions: graded potentials commonly involve sodium in, potassium out or chloride in; the action potential is sodium in then potassium out.
Size: graded potentials are a few millivolts; the action potential is about 100 millivolts from rest to peak.
Stimulus strength: graded potential size varies with it; action potential size does not.
Travel: graded potentials fade within a short distance; action potentials travel the full axon without fading.
Threshold: not required for a graded potential, required for an action potential.
Refractory period: none for graded potentials, present for action potentials.
Coding: graded potentials code strength by amplitude, action potentials code it by frequency.
distinctions: Both signals are changes in membrane voltage, so the difference lies in the channels, the size, the distance and the all or nothing rule.
misconceptions: Filling in refractory period for the graded potential row. Graded potentials can be summed immediately, which is exactly why summation works.

essentials: Key voltages are rest near minus 70 millivolts, threshold near minus 55 millivolts, peak near plus 30 millivolts, and the undershoot near minus 80 millivolts.
Rising phase: voltage gated sodium channels open and sodium rushes into the cell down both its concentration gradient and the electrical pull.
Peak: sodium channels inactivate and voltage gated potassium channels are opening.
Falling phase: potassium leaves the cell through voltage gated potassium channels while sodium entry has stopped.
Undershoot: the slow potassium channels stay open a little too long, so extra potassium leaves and the membrane dips below the resting potential before the channels close.

The voltage gated sodium channel has an activation gate and an inactivation gate. At rest the activation gate is closed and the inactivation gate is open; at threshold the activation gate opens and sodium flows; at the peak the inactivation gate swings shut; during the falling phase the activation gate closes again and the inactivation gate reopens only once the membrane has repolarized.
distinctions: Closed and inactivated are different states. A closed channel can open; an inactivated one cannot until the membrane repolarizes.
Sodium channels are fast and potassium channels are slow, which is why the rising phase is steep and the recovery is drawn out.
misconceptions: Saying potassium enters during repolarization. Potassium leaves, which is why the inside becomes negative again.
Saying the pump causes repolarization. Open potassium channels do.
key.where: Section 4, phases of the action potential

essentials: Sodium inactivation gates held open: sodium keeps entering, so the membrane stays depolarized near the peak and the action potential is greatly prolonged instead of returning to rest promptly.
Slowed potassium channels: the falling phase begins later and takes longer, so the action potential is wider, and the undershoot is delayed.
Half the sodium channels blocked: the rising phase is slower and the peak is lower, and a weak stimulus may no longer reach threshold at all.
Outside sodium halved: the inward driving force for sodium falls, so the peak is lower, while threshold may still be reached if enough channels open.
distinctions: Changes in sodium affect the rising phase and the peak; changes in potassium affect the falling phase and the undershoot.
A lower peak is a problem of driving force or channel number; a longer spike is a problem of gate timing.
misconceptions: Expecting a partial sodium block to shrink every action potential a little. Spikes that still reach threshold are close to full size; the stronger effect is that fewer stimuli succeed at all.
key.where: Section 4, channel changes and the tracing

essentials: 1. A stimulus opens gated channels and depolarizes the membrane toward threshold.
2. At threshold near minus 55 millivolts, voltage gated sodium activation gates open.
3. Sodium moves into the cell, and that depolarization opens still more sodium channels, which is a positive feedback cycle.
4. The membrane rises steeply to about plus 30 millivolts.
5. Sodium inactivation gates close, ending sodium entry.
6. Slow voltage gated potassium channels finish opening.
7. Potassium moves out of the cell and the membrane repolarizes toward the resting potential.
8. Potassium channels close late, so extra potassium leaves and the membrane undershoots to about minus 80 millivolts.
9. Potassium channels close, sodium inactivation gates reopen, and leak channels plus the sodium potassium pump return the membrane to minus 70 millivolts.
distinctions: The positive feedback of step 3 is what makes the action potential all or nothing.
Inactivation of sodium channels and opening of potassium channels are separate events that happen at about the same time.
misconceptions: Putting potassium channel opening before sodium inactivation as the cause of the peak. Both contribute, but the peak is set by sodium entry stopping.

essentials: Recognize: the drug blocks the action potential itself, not the resting potential and not the graded potential, so the sensory neuron can still respond locally but cannot send a signal.

Explain: a blocked voltage gated sodium channel cannot pass sodium, so the rising phase never develops; without a rising phase the membrane cannot depolarize the next patch of axon to threshold, so nothing is regenerated along the axon and no signal reaches the brain.

Differentiate: small diameter axons, including the thinly myelinated and unmyelinated pain fibers, are blocked first because they have less membrane to block and a smaller safety margin, while the large myelinated axons that carry pressure and the motor axons that move the jaw keep conducting longer.

Investigate: touch the gum with a sharp probe and ask whether it feels sharp or only like pressure, and compare the treated side with the untreated side using the same light touch; loss of sharpness with pressure preserved shows the block has reached the pain fibers but not the large touch fibers.
Decide: yes, the resting membrane potential of the blocked neuron is still normal.

Justify: the resting potential is set by potassium leak channels, the trapped negative proteins and the sodium potassium pump, and none of those are affected by a drug that binds only voltage gated sodium channels, so the cell still rests near minus 70 millivolts while being unable to fire.
distinctions: A cell can have a perfectly normal resting potential and still be unable to produce an action potential.
Fiber size and myelination explain the order in which sensations disappear.
misconceptions: Thinking the anesthetic kills the neuron. The block is reversible, which is why normal sensation returns in about two hours.
Thinking the drug blocks the brain's perception rather than the axon's signal.
key.where: Section 4, voltage gated sodium channels, with Section 6 for fiber size

essentials: The absolute refractory period covers the rising phase and most of the falling phase; no stimulus of any strength can produce a second action potential during it.
During the absolute refractory period the sodium activation gates have opened and the inactivation gates are closed, and the closed inactivation gate is the reason no second spike is possible.
The relative refractory period covers the end of the falling phase and the undershoot; a second action potential is possible but needs a stronger than usual stimulus.
During the relative refractory period potassium channels are still open, so potassium is still leaving and the membrane is more negative than rest, which puts threshold further away.

Sodium channels must reset, meaning the inactivation gate reopens while the activation gate closes, and that reset requires the membrane to repolarize back toward the resting range near minus 70 millivolts.
distinctions: Absolute means impossible; relative means harder.
The absolute period is about channel state, while the relative period is mostly about voltage being further from threshold.
misconceptions: Blaming the refractory period on depleted ion gradients. One action potential moves very few ions; the cause is channel state and membrane voltage.

essentials: The patch just behind the advancing spike has sodium channels in the inactivated state, so it cannot fire again immediately, and the signal therefore moves only forward.
The absolute refractory period sets the maximum firing rate, since a neuron cannot fire again until it has passed.
With an absolute refractory period near one millisecond, the ceiling is roughly 1000 action potentials per second, and real neurons fire well below that.

Without refractory periods, signals would spread in both directions along axons and summed stimuli would produce continuous uncontrolled firing, so timing information and orderly muscle contraction would be lost.
distinctions: One way conduction comes from refractoriness behind the spike, not from any one way property of the channels themselves.
Maximum firing rate and conduction speed are different things; refractory periods set the first, myelin and diameter set the second.
misconceptions: Thinking the axon is built to carry signals in only one direction. An axon stimulated in the middle in the laboratory conducts both ways; in the body the signal starts at one end.
key.where: Section 5, one way conduction and firing limits

essentials: Myelin is a fatty wrapping made by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system and by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system.
Myelin insulates the membrane so charge does not leak out, and it leaves the covered membrane with very few open channels.
Nodes of Ranvier are the bare gaps between myelin segments, and voltage gated sodium channels are clustered there.

The action potential is regenerated only at the nodes and the depolarization spreads quickly through the cytoplasm under each myelin segment, so the signal appears to jump from node to node; this is saltatory conduction.
Conduction is faster in axons that are myelinated and in axons that are wider.
A large myelinated axon conducts at roughly 100 meters per second, while a small unmyelinated axon conducts at roughly 1 meter per second.
distinctions: Myelin does not make the action potential bigger; it makes the spread between nodes faster.
Diameter helps because a wider axon offers less internal resistance to the spread of charge.
misconceptions: Picturing the action potential physically leaping through the air between nodes. The local current flows through the cytoplasm and the spike is regenerated at each node.
Thinking myelin covers the whole axon continuously. The nodes are essential gaps, not defects.

essentials: Losing patches of myelin slows conduction, and where the loss is wide the signal may fail to reach the next node at all, so sensation or movement served by that axon becomes slow, patchy or absent.

The signal can stop completely because the membrane under the former sheath has very few voltage gated sodium channels, so a bare stretch cannot regenerate the spike and the depolarization leaks away before reaching the next node.
Myelin gives speed in a thin axon, while widening the axon gives speed at a large cost in space, so myelin lets a nerve pack many fast axons into a small cross section.
Sharp, well localized pain travels on thinly myelinated axons, and dull aching pain travels on unmyelinated axons, which is why sharp pain arrives first.
distinctions: Slowed conduction and failed conduction are different outcomes, set by how much sheath is lost at one place.
Demyelination leaves the axon itself alive, which is why some function can return if the sheath is repaired.
misconceptions: Assuming loss of myelin cuts the axon. The axon is intact; the insulation is what has gone.
key.where: Section 6, conduction speed and loss of myelin

essentials: The absolute refractory period exists because the inactivation gates of the voltage gated sodium channels are shut and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes.
distinctions: Channel state explains the absolute period; a more negative membrane voltage explains the relative period.
misconceptions: Attributing refractoriness to used up gradients or to pump activity.
key.why_right: Once the inactivation gate closes at the peak, the channel is unavailable no matter how strong the stimulus, and it resets only after the membrane repolarizes, which is exactly what makes the period absolute.
why_wrong: A single action potential moves only a tiny fraction of the sodium and potassium present, so the gradients are still essentially intact and the pump is not the limiting factor.
A membrane more negative than rest describes the undershoot, and that is the relative refractory period, when a strong stimulus can still work.
The voltage gated potassium channels are open rather than closed during this part of the tracing, and their opening is what repolarizes the membrane.

essentials: Myelin speeds conduction by preventing charge leak across the covered membrane, so depolarization reaches the next node quickly, and the sodium channels clustered at the nodes regenerate the spike there.
distinctions: Speed comes from faster passive spread between nodes, not from a bigger or faster individual action potential.
misconceptions: Thinking myelin adds channels or energy along the axon rather than insulating it.
key.why_right: Insulation keeps the local current inside the axon so it spreads rapidly to the next node, where clustered voltage gated sodium channels fire a fresh action potential, and this node to node pattern is saltatory conduction.
why_wrong: Myelin is insulation made of membrane lipid and does not supply ATP; the pump gets its ATP from the axon's own metabolism.
Sodium channels in a myelinated axon are clustered at the nodes rather than spread evenly, and spreading them out evenly would slow conduction.
The absolute refractory period depends on sodium channel gating and is not shortened by myelin, and firing rate is a separate matter from conduction speed.
